periods.activity_title: Opening the Spice Cabinet: Pre-Reading and First Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.95): read the extract about Daadi's grandmother and discuss three questions.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to name three spices used at home and briefly share one use each family member knows. This activates prior knowledge before the text is opened.
Teacher reads Daadi's letter aloud with students following in their textbooks; pause at each spice name to let students locate the Hindi/regional name on the matching chart on p.93–94.

Guided discussion on "Let us read" (p.95): where Daadi's grandmother found the cures, an example of a weather-related illness, and what the relationship between Daadi and her grandmother tells us about how knowledge travels.
Quick paired share — each pair names one spice from the letter and its benefit; teacher confirms and closes the first reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The letter form of the text is important: draw students' attention to the greeting, the body, and the closing so they recognise informational content delivered through a personal voice. A common difficulty is mapping the English spice name to its regional equivalent — the picture-matching activity on p.93 supports this and should not be rushed. Students who miss the intergenerational link between Daadi, her grandmother, and the children may need a second prompt: ask who taught whom.

periods.activity_title: Reading for Meaning: Comprehension and Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.95): fill in the blanks about methi seeds.
Let us discuss (p.95): circle/identify the spice not useful for body pain.
Let us discuss (p.95): explain why Daadi asked the children to share cures.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.95): write Daadi's final advice to Vikram and Vaibhavi.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap of Daadi's letter: teacher asks students to call out the spices mentioned and what each heals, building a quick spoken list on the board.
Students complete the fill-in-the-blank item about methi seeds (p.95) individually, then compare with a partner; teacher confirms the two answers — blood sugar and body weight.
Whole-class task: teacher reads the four spice options aloud for the body-pain question (p.95); students justify their choice before the answer is confirmed together.

Class discussion on why Daadi wanted the children to share the cures with friends (p.95), drawing out the idea of intergenerational and community transmission of knowledge; students write one sentence summing up their answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Daadi's descriptions of each spice aloud, students now apply that information to closed and open questions. Watch for students who confuse the body-pain question — fennel seeds and carom seeds aid digestion rather than relieve pain, which is the distinction the item targets. The homework asks students to revisit the letter's closing lines; it is self-contained and needs no class preparation.

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeper: Reflection on Traditional Knowledge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.95): explain how natural cures pass across generations.
Let us think and reflect (p.95): extended response on why knowing spice-healing properties matters.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to share any home remedy they know, linking it to the idea of knowledge passed down through families — this connects to Daadi's letter without requiring prior class work.

Paired discussion on "Let us think and reflect" (p.95): how do we know natural cures travel from one generation to the next? Pairs share one piece of evidence from the letter; teacher records key points on the board.

Students write an extended response (p.95) on why knowing the healing properties of spices is worthwhile; teacher circulates, prompting students to include at least one specific spice as an example and to state a personal or community reason.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through Daadi's factual descriptions of individual spices, students now move to the reflective strand — asking why this knowledge matters rather than what it says. A common gap is that students repeat factual details instead of giving a reflective reason; prompt them to think about a world without easy access to medicines. The extended response should be a short paragraph of three to four sentences, not a list.
materials: Board or chart paper for recording shared points

periods.activity_title: The Wonder Herb: Listening to Tulsi

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.98): complete the Tulsi fact sheet while listening to the passage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Tulsi by asking whether anyone has the plant at home and what they know about it; this primes attention without pre-teaching the content of the listening passage.
Teacher distributes or reads out the fact-sheet template (p.98) with students; they identify the eight blank slots before listening so they know what to listen for.

Teacher reads the Tulsi passage aloud at a steady pace; students fill in the fact sheet as they listen. A second reading is given at a slightly slower pace for students to check or complete missed blanks.

Whole-class verification: teacher calls on students for each numbered blank in sequence; confirms answers against the passage and clarifies any confusion about the basil family, glucose/cholesterol, or anti-bacterial properties.

periods.teacher_notes: The Tulsi passage is the chapter's only listening text and introduces a herb not covered in Daadi's letter, so students have no prior textbook anchor for most facts. Read the passage at a natural spoken pace — not slower than normal speech — so that the skill of listening under real conditions is practised. Students often mishear 'basil family' as a place name; write it on the board after the second reading.
materials: Listening passage text (p.102) for teacher reading

periods.activity_title: Be the Spice: Oral Introduction with Headband

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.96): make a spicy headband and introduce yourself as a chosen spice.

time_bands.activity: Students choose a spice from Daadi's letter, cut a paper strip for their headband, make a small labelled card with the spice name, and attach it — all craft steps completed within this time band before any speaking begins.

Teacher models the spice introduction using the six prompts (name, part of plant, colour, texture, taste, benefits), then demonstrates once with a chosen spice so students hear the expected register and length before they speak.

Students take turns introducing themselves as their spice to the class; teacher uses a brief checklist on the board (name / part / colour / texture / taste / benefits) to help the audience track each speaker's coverage and offer one positive comment.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about the spices' properties in Daadi's letter, students now speak from the spice's perspective — a first-person register that encourages confident, playful delivery. Students who hesitate can be paired to present together as 'two forms of the same spice.' Keep the audience engaged by asking one question per presenter rather than applauding silently.
materials: Paper strips (approximately 2 cm wide, one per student)

periods.activity_title: Completing Natural Cures: Guided Writing with Phrases

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.99): complete the two natural-cure recipes by selecting the correct phrases from the box.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the scenario: Vikram's grandmother's letter was damaged by rain and words are missing. Students read the seven phrases in the box (p.99) and identify which two are not needed, discussing as a class.
Students complete the first natural cure — the ginger and honey remedy for cough — individually, then compare choices with a partner before the class confirms the correct phrases together.

Students complete the second natural cure — the long pepper, dried ginger, basil, and cardamom powder recipe — following the same individual-then-paired process; teacher confirms answers and reads both completed cures aloud.
Brief closure: teacher asks which cure students found harder to complete and why, reinforcing that the phrase-box strategy involves reading for contextual fit rather than guessing.

periods.teacher_notes: Having listened to the Tulsi passage and read Daadi's letter, students now engage with a functional writing form — procedural instructions. The key difficulty is distinguishing which phrase fits which blank by meaning rather than word length; prompt students to read the full sentence with each candidate phrase before deciding. Both cures should be read aloud in their completed form so students can hear whether the text sounds natural.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Tulsi: From Fact Sheet to Paragraph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.100): write a short informational paragraph on Tulsi using the completed fact sheet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes a sample fact-sheet skeleton on the board (eight labelled slots: family, origin, known as, decreases, treats, used in, eaten as, calms) and asks students to populate it from memory before consulting any notes.
Teacher models converting two fact-sheet entries into connected sentences using linking words (because, also, in addition); students see the difference between a list and a paragraph before writing.

Students write their paragraph on Tulsi (p.100), aiming for five to six sentences that cover the herb's origin, properties, and uses; teacher circulates and prompts students who are simply copying fact-sheet entries verbatim to connect ideas with a linking word.
Two or three volunteers read their paragraphs aloud; class identifies one strong linking phrase in each paragraph and the teacher notes it on the board as a shared model.

periods.teacher_notes: Having completed the Tulsi fact sheet during the listening task, students now use that information as the basis for a short informational paragraph — a functional writing form. The most common issue is that students produce a numbered list rather than connected prose; the modelling step is essential to distinguish the two. Encourage students to begin with a topic sentence that names Tulsi and its popular title ('the Queen of Herbs') before listing properties.

periods.activity_title: Spice Profiles and Modal Verbs: Language in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.96): complete the spice-property table — part of plant, colour, texture, taste.
Let us learn (p.97): match six modal verbs to their functions in Column B.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.97): complete the dialogue using any four modals, each used only once.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the spice-property table (p.96) for six spices — turmeric, fenugreek, cinnamon, clove, black pepper, cardamom — filling in part of plant, colour, texture, and taste; teacher circulates and resolves uncertainty by directing students to the relevant sentences in Daadi's letter.

Teacher writes six sentences from Daadi's letter on the board, each containing a modal verb (may, should, can, must, need to, used to), underlines the modal, and asks students to notice what each one signals before formally matching Column A to Column B (p.97).

Class confirms the six matches together; teacher explains the distinction between 'must' (compulsion) and 'need to' (necessity) using one further example from everyday life, then sets the dialogue-completion task as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The spice-property table draws on the descriptive vocabulary of Daadi's letter — root, bark, leaves, flower buds, seeds, bitter, sweet, spicy — so students should have their textbooks open to the relevant pages. For the modal-verb matching, students often conflate 'should' (advice) with 'must' (compulsion); use Daadi's own closing advice ('you should consult an elder') as the anchor example. The dialogue-completion homework is self-contained and uses the same six modals just matched.
materials: Board for writing sample sentences with modals

periods.activity_title: Spice Riddles: Reading, Guessing and Composing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.100): solve the two riddles to identify the spices they describe.
Let us explore (p.100): fill in the blanks to complete the fenugreek riddle.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.100): write an original riddle about a spice; share with a family member to guess.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads both riddles on p.100 aloud while students listen with books closed; after each riddle, students write their guess on a slip of paper before the answer is revealed — this keeps guessing independent.

Class discusses the clues in each riddle — which words pointed to 'tummy' for one and 'underground root' and '4000 years' for the other — linking the riddle language back to Daadi's descriptions of the same spices.

Students fill in the three blanks of the fenugreek riddle (p.100) individually, read the completed riddle aloud in pairs to check that it rhymes and makes sense, then receive the homework: write one original riddle about any spice from the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about the healing properties of spices in Daadi's letter, students now encounter the same knowledge in a playful wordplay form. The riddle-completing task highlights that spice descriptions — colour, taste, benefit — are exactly the clues a riddle uses, reinforcing descriptive vocabulary. For the homework riddle, encourage students to pick a spice whose colour, texture, or benefit is distinctive so that the riddle has a clear answer.
materials: Small slips of paper for silent guessing

periods.activity_title: Sense and Explore: Spices Beyond the Page

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.100): identify spices by smell and touch with eyes closed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher places small labelled containers of four or five spices (turmeric, cumin, cardamom, clove, fenugreek) at the front; students observe them briefly with eyes open so they know what the candidates are.

Students close their eyes; teacher passes each container around in sequence — students smell, then feel the texture, and write their guess on paper without speaking. After all containers have circulated, guesses are revealed and discussed as a class.

Reflection circle: each student shares one surprising thing they noticed about a spice through smell or touch that they could not have known from reading alone — linking sensory experience to the informational text and its descriptions of texture and aroma.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about spice properties and composed riddles using descriptive language, students now experience those properties directly through the senses — a hands-on extension that grounds the chapter's informational content in embodied knowledge. Arrange spices in sealed containers so that texture can be felt through the lid or through a small bag; direct handling of raw spices may not suit all classrooms. Students who cannot participate in the smelling activity for health reasons may describe the spice from memory instead.
materials: Small sealed containers of turmeric, cumin, cardamom, clove, and fenugreek (or a subset the school can provide)

periods.activity_title: From Daadi's Kitchen to Ours: Whole-Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Teacher-led recall web on the board: students call out every spice from Daadi's letter and the Tulsi listening passage; teacher maps each to its key benefit, building a shared visual that draws together the chapter's informational content.

Small-group discussion (groups of three): each group compares Daadi's letter as an informational source with the Tulsi listening passage — what made each form effective, what each left out, and whether modal verbs ('should', 'must', 'can') appeared in both. Groups share one insight aloud.

Individual writing task (new, self-contained): students write a short advisory note of four to five sentences addressed to a younger sibling, recommending two spices from the chapter for a common ailment and explaining why, using at least two modal verbs correctly.

Two or three volunteers read their advisory notes aloud; class identifies the modal verbs used and checks whether the informational content is accurate — a brief peer-verification that closes the chapter on both language and content.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the chapter's full range of content — Daadi's letter, the Tulsi listening passage, the spice-property vocabulary, modal verbs, and the riddle and sensory activities. The advisory-note writing task is new and complete within this unit: it begins, develops, and ends here. Prompt students who struggle to choose a spice by directing them to the benefit web built at the start of the unit.
materials: Board or chart paper for the benefit web

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and interprets factual and inferential information using an informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Daadi's letter on ten kitchen spices, their healing properties, intergenerational knowledge transmission.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Daadi's letter. Write True or False for each statement.
1. Daadi learnt about natural cures from her own grandmother.
2. Ginger has been used in cooking for over 2000 years.
3. Daadi advises Vikram and Vaibhavi to share the natural cures with their friends.
4. Fennel seeds and carom seeds are recommended by Daadi for relieving toothache.

options.text: Daadi advises Vikram and Vaibhavi to share the natural cures with their friends.
Daadi learnt about natural cures from her own grandmother.
Fennel seeds and carom seeds are recommended by Daadi for relieving toothache.
Ginger has been used in cooking for over 2000 years.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Daadi says she learnt the cures from her grandmother when she was a child.
2. False — Ginger has been used in cooking for over 4000 years, not 2000.
3. True — Daadi's closing advice asks Vikram and Vaibhavi to share these remedies with their friends.
4. False — Daadi recommends cinnamon (dalchini) and clove (laung) for toothache; fennel seeds and carom seeds aid digestion.

items.item_stem: In her letter, Daadi says she learnt the natural cures from her grandmother and now passes them on to Vikram and Vaibhavi. What does this tell us about the way traditional knowledge travels through a family? Give one specific example from the letter to support your answer.

expected_elements: States that knowledge passes from one generation to the next.
Uses Daadi–grandmother or Daadi–grandchildren link as evidence.
Shows the letter itself is an act of sharing traditional knowledge.
Names at least one specific spice or cure from the letter.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. basil 2. north central India 3. Queen 4. cholesterol 5. hand 6. tea

items.item_stem: The passage describes Tulsi as 'the Queen of Herbs.' Based on what you heard, give two reasons why Tulsi might deserve this title. Write your answer in two sentences.

expected_elements: Names at least two distinct benefits (e.g., decreases glucose and cholesterol).
References one product or use (sanitiser, mouthwash, toothpaste, or tea).
Connects the breadth of uses to the idea of Tulsi being exceptional.
Writes in complete sentences without copying the passage verbatim.

In your introduction, tell the class your name, which part of the plant you come from, your colour and texture, your taste, and one healing benefit you provide.

expected_elements: Names the spice and its plant part clearly.
Describes colour, texture, and taste accurately.
States one specific healing benefit from Daadi's letter.
Speaks in first person throughout the introduction.

items.item_stem: Daadi tells Vikram and Vaibhavi that they should share natural cures with their friends. Imagine you are Vikram or Vaibhavi speaking to a friend who has a cold. Recommend one spice from the letter, explain how to use it, and give your friend a reason to trust this remedy. Speak for about one minute.

expected_elements: Names the spice and a specific use for cold or related ailment.
Explains how to prepare or consume it.
Gives a reason for trusting the remedy (e.g., Daadi's experience, long tradition).
Uses a persuasive or caring tone appropriate to speaking to a friend.

items.item_stem: Daadi's letter describes several natural cures. Imagine you are writing a short entry for a school health notice board. Write four to five sentences giving a simple natural remedy for one common ailment (such as a cold, an upset stomach, or a toothache) using information from Daadi's letter. Include the name of the spice, how to use it, and who would benefit from it.

expected_elements: Names a specific spice and links it to a matching ailment from the letter.
States how the spice is to be used or prepared.
Identifies who would benefit (e.g., someone with a cold, a student with an upset stomach).
Uses clear, simple notice-board language without bullet points or headers.

items.item_stem: Vikram and Vaibhavi wrote back to Daadi to thank her. Write a short letter from one of them to Daadi in which you describe how you used one of the spice remedies she suggested, how it helped you, and what you will do with this knowledge. Write six to eight sentences in informal letter format.

expected_elements: Uses informal letter format: greeting, body, and closing.
Names a specific remedy from Daadi's letter and describes using it.
Explains the effect of the remedy on their health.
States an intention to share the knowledge with someone else, echoing Daadi's advice.

items.source_context: Spice-property vocabulary (part of plant, texture, taste); six modal verbs and their functions from Daadi's letter.
items.item_stem:
Daadi uses modal verbs throughout her letter to give advice, express ability, and describe past habits. Read the sentences below and fill in each blank with the correct modal verb (should, can, must, used to, need to). Use each modal only once.
(1) Daadi _______ prepare turmeric milk every evening when she was young.
(2) You _______ consult an elder before using any natural cure, says Daadi.
(3) Black pepper _______ help with digestion and relieve body pain.
(4) When you have a cold, you _______ drink ginger tea regularly for relief.
(5) You _______ share these remedies with your friends, Daadi told the children.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. used to 2. must 3. can 4. need to 5. should

items.source_context: Spice riddles — guessing, completing, composing; sensory identification of spices by smell and touch.
items.item_stem:
Read the riddle below and write the name of the spice it describes. Then explain in one sentence which clue in the riddle helped you identify it.

'I am yellow and ground from a root,
In kitchens I am famous, in healing absolute.
I ease your pain and warm your blood,
A pinch of me in milk is always good.
Who am I?'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The spice is turmeric (haldi). The clue 'yellow and ground from a root' combined with 'pinch of me in milk' and the reference to relieving pain matches Daadi's description of turmeric improving energy and reducing body pain.

items.source_context: Spice riddles — guessing, completing, composing; sensory identification of spices by smell and touch.
items.item_stem: Choose any one spice from Daadi's letter that you find interesting. Write a riddle of four lines about that spice. Your riddle must include at least one clue about the spice's appearance or smell, one clue about a healing benefit mentioned in the letter, and end with the question 'Who am I?' Do not name the spice anywhere in your riddle.

expected_elements: Includes a clue about appearance, colour, texture, or smell of the chosen spice.
Includes a clue about a healing benefit drawn from Daadi's letter.
Does not name the spice directly anywhere in the riddle.
Ends with 'Who am I?' and is written in four lines.
